analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare-based public health insurance option and lets Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices.
analysis.headline: The public-option bill died in committee: it was referred to three House committees in June 2018 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The Choose Medicare Act would have created "Medicare Part E" — a government-run health plan that anyone not on Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP could buy on the insurance exchanges, and that employers could voluntarily offer to workers [S2][S3]. It also would have capped out-of-pocket costs for seniors in traditional Medicare at $6,700 a year, required the government to negotiate Medicare drug prices directly with manufacturers, enlarged ACA premium subsidies (up to incomes of 600% of poverty, measured against gold-level plans), deepened cost-sharing help for lower-income buyers, and put $10 billion into a reinsurance program to steady the individual insurance market [S3][S2]. It was referred to three House committees, sent to two subcommittees, and never advanced again [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: People buying their own insurance would gain a public plan on the exchanges, bigger subsidies (extended to households earning up to 600% of the poverty line and pegged to gold plans rather than the cheaper silver plans), and deeper cost-sharing reductions for lower incomes [S3 §2, §6, §7]. Uninsured workers at employers that don't offer affordable coverage would be referred to exchange navigators who help them enroll [S3 §3]. Seniors in traditional Medicare would get a hard annual out-of-pocket cap starting at $6,700 in 2020 and lower drug prices through government negotiation, with a fallback to the lower VA or federal supply schedule price if talks failed [S3 §4, §5]. Women in states restricting abortion coverage would gain a plan that covers reproductive services regardless of state law [S3 §2(b)].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Exchange buyers, Medicare beneficiaries, uninsured workers

how_it_helps.text: Creates Medicare Part E, a public health plan available to individuals, small employers, and large employers on the exchanges, with gold-level coverage and all Medicare-covered benefits, so people without affordable employer coverage could buy a government option alongside private plans
Caps annual out-of-pocket cost-sharing for traditional Medicare beneficiaries — who currently have no limit — at $6,700 starting in 2020, adjusted each year for medical inflation

Requires the Health and Human Services Secretary to negotiate prices for Medicare Part D prescription drugs, and if negotiation fails after a year, to set the price at the lower of what the VA pays or the federal supply schedule price

Enlarges ACA premium tax credits by extending eligibility from 400% to 600% of the poverty line and pegging the subsidy benchmark to gold-level plans instead of silver, and deepens cost-sharing reductions so low-income enrollees' plans cover up to 94% of costs
Requires employers that do not offer affordable, adequate coverage to refer full-time employees to exchange navigators who help people enroll, and funds navigator capacity
Requires every Medicare Part E plan to cover abortion and other reproductive services and bars states from prohibiting that coverage
Appropriates $10 billion for a three-year state reinsurance program to lower individual-market premiums, and $2 billion in start-up funding plus reserves for the public plans

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the start-up ($2 billion), initial reserves, the $10 billion reinsurance program, and the larger premium tax credits and navigator grants [S3 §2(h), §3, §6, §8]. Prescription drug manufacturers would lose revenue from government-negotiated Medicare prices [S3 §5]. Private insurers would face direct competition from the public plan in every market segment [S3 §2]. Doctors, hospitals, and other providers would be paid under rates negotiated between the Medicare rate floor and the average exchange rate ceiling — potentially less than private rates for some services [S3 §2(e)]. Younger, healthier employees in large firms could see premium increases as the bill extends community-rating rules (limits on how much premiums can vary by age or health) from the small-group to the large-group market [S3 §9].
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, drug makers, and private insurers

drawbacks.text: The public plan must fully finance its own benefit and administrative costs through premiums, and the government's provider rates are capped at no higher than average exchange rates, so the plan's promised savings and stability depend on untested negotiations; the bill adds $2 billion in start-up money, initial reserves, and $10 billion in reinsurance spending in the meantime

Extending the small-group rating rules to the large-group market limits how much premiums can vary by age, which lowers premiums for older and sicker employees but raises them for younger, healthier workers at large employers

Requiring the public plan to cover abortion and barring states from prohibiting it was the bill's most politically contentious provision, and the bill's own 'sense of Congress' section calling for an end to all private-market coverage restrictions guaranteed opposition from anti-abortion lawmakers

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and large for identifiable groups: a permanent out-of-pocket cap for seniors, government drug-price negotiation, a public plan option, and much richer subsidies for working-age buyers [S3]. The costs are real but mostly fiscal — new appropriations and bigger tax credits — with the heaviest losses falling on drug makers and insurers rather than ordinary people; the main design weakness is that the public plan's self-financing premium model was untested, and the large-group rating change could modestly shift costs onto younger workers. On balance, the bill was a substantial help to ordinary people funded substantially by concentrated interests and general revenue.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in three House committees and then two subcommittees for the rest of the 115th Congress, and it died in January 2019 without ever getting a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Cedric Richmond of Louisiana introduced the Choose Medicare Act on June 14, 2018, joined by five original cosponsors

The bill was referred the same day to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce — a multi-committee referral that splits jurisdiction and makes advancement harder
Within six weeks it was sent to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and in October 2018 to the Education and the Workforce Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
Ten House Democrats had cosponsored the bill by the end, but no Republican sponsored it and no committee took up the bill before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prescription drug manufacturers and private health insurers came out ahead: a government-negotiated drug pricing regime and a public insurance competitor never advanced, so the existing pricing and market structure continued unchanged. Medicare beneficiaries and exchange buyers gained nothing because the out-of-pocket cap, subsidies, and public plan never became law.

for.name: Rep. Cedric Richmond
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Choose Medicare Act and assembled five original cosponsors from across the House

for.name: 10 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Reps. Huffman, Lowenthal, Jeffries, Eddie Bernice Johnson, and DeSaulnier

against.name: House Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce Committees (Republican majorities)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittees and never held a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill was never reported out or scheduled for floor action before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: Every supporter in the record — the sponsor and all 10 cosponsors — was a House Democrat, no Republican cosponsored, and the bill died in committees controlled by the Republican House majority without a single recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill strikes the 'noninterference' clause that forbids Medicare from negotiating and requires the government to negotiate Part D drug prices, with a fallback to the lower of VA or federal supply schedule prices if talks fail. That directly cuts manufacturer revenue on Medicare's largest drug program.

A government-run plan would compete with private insurers in the individual, small-group, and large-group markets, pressuring their prices and enrollment. The $10 billion reinsurance program would simultaneously shore up their individual-market risk pools. The industry's core interest in avoiding a public competitor ran against what exchange buyers stood to gain.

Providers would gain millions of newly subsidized customers, but payment rates would be negotiated between a Medicare-rate floor and an average-exchange-rate ceiling, and every existing Medicare provider would automatically become a participating provider at those rates. Some providers would earn less per service than under private coverage.

Employers could voluntarily buy into Medicare Part E or have the government administer their self-funded plans, adding a cheaper option to the benefits market, but extending community-rating rules to large groups could raise premiums for younger workforces. Employers that offer unaffordable coverage would face a new obligation to refer employees to exchange navigators.
